stageLabel: A mathematical manuscript written under secrecy and reviewed
shapeSentences: A knowledgeable, self-taught mathematical reader fears she is not qualified to write, agrees to try under secrecy, and works through interruptions before an expert review offers praise and corrections.
A published book reaches mathematical students, while further criticism and the difficulty of its mathematics prevent a claim of universal access.

facets.emotionalCore: Fear that self-acquired knowledge is inadequate for a demanding writing task, followed by nervousness during examination of the manuscript.
facets.decisionShape: Agree to do her best on condition of secrecy and destruction of the manuscript if it fails.
facets.triggerEvent: A request to explain advanced mathematical astronomy exceeds what she believes she is qualified to write.
facets.agencyState: She can agree, arrange family work, write around interruptions, and submit a manuscript; protected time, expert judgment, and readers' mathematical preparation remain outside her sole control.

biographicalFacts: A letter dated March 27, 1827 from Henry Brougham to William Somerville asks for an explanation of Laplace's Mécanique Céleste that introduces its mathematical methods and a deeper account for mathematical readers. It proposes concealing the writer's identity. A few days after the letter, Brougham visited Mary Somerville at Chelsea. He and her husband urged her to make the attempt. She explained that readers would need differential and integral calculus, that preliminary mechanics and astronomy problems required proof, and that she would need diagrams absent from Laplace's work. Mary Somerville was born December 26, 1780. She was forty-six at the March 27, 1827 request and the visit a few days later. She was fifty at the November 2, 1831 acknowledgment of her published book. Somerville was surprised by the request. She thought Brougham had mistaken the extent of her knowledge and that her self-acquired knowledge was inferior to university-educated men's knowledge. She believed writing on the subject would be presumptuous. During the visit she said she feared being incapable of the task. These are her later recollection of her own assessments, not proof of actual mathematical inferiority. In the conversation Somerville said she would do her best, conditional on secrecy and on destruction of the manuscript if it failed. This is a remembered agreement to attempt the work, not an account of a manuscript actually being destroyed. She rose early and arranged her children's and family affairs to allow writing afterwards, with many interruptions. Visitors came to see her at Chelsea and she felt receiving them was necessary. Sometimes they arrived in the middle of a difficult problem. She contrasted men's ability to protect business time with women's inability to claim that excuse. She learned to leave and resume a subject. Her little room lacked a fireplace, so she wrote in the drawing-room in winter. She frequently hid her papers when the visitor bell rang, to conceal her work. Martha Somerville remembers her mother teaching the children for a few hours daily and then continuing mathematical work while they remained in the room. She answered their questions and returned to work, but could also become impatient when they were inattentive. This is the daughter's later remembered account of ordinary family work, not a date-specific scene. Writing occupied a considerable time. Somerville continued social visits, dinners, evening parties, and occasional theatre visits. When the manuscript was finished she sent it to Brougham asking for thorough examination and criticism, and destruction if it was a failure. Somerville says she was very nervous during examination of the manuscript, surprised and gratified that Herschel found so few errors, and happy and proud because of the letter he wrote. She preserved the letter. This is late recollection of her reaction and retention; it does not specify the letter's date, a reading place, or an immediate storage gesture. The first reproduced Herschel review letter says he read the manuscript with pleasure and admiration and considered it useful. He marks an obscure part of an explanation concerning virtual velocities and a small point on page six, asking her to look at the former again. It is undated in the book and does not claim all revisions were completed. In a later letter dated February 23, 1830, Herschel advises greater clarity, fullness, and order, recommends at least doubling the first part, and says her familiarity led to passing over difficulties beginners could not overcome. The letter makes specific criticisms of how mathematical principles are explained. Its existence proves further criticism, not that every recommendation was followed. Mechanism of the Heavens was published in 1831. Whewell's November 2, 1831 letter thanks Somerville for a book and copies for the Philosophical Society and college library. He says young mathematicians would have easy access and benefit when able to read it. Somerville describes the preface as the only part of her published mathematical book intelligible to the general reader. This is a characterization of the book's content, not a claim that separate preface copies had been printed by November 1831. The recalled separate printing follows the February 14, 1832 letter and is outside this episode. Mary Somerville wrote explanations of mathematical astronomy, including how gravity relates to the motions of the planets.
sources: Mary Somerville, Personal Recollections, from Early Life to Old Age, edited by Martha Somerville (London: John Murray, 1874, fifth thousand). Late-life autobiographical recollections and contemporary correspondence reproduced by the editor. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/27747/27747-h/27747-h.htm Chapter I p. 8 (birth); Chapter XI pp. 161–172 (March 27, 1827 request, visit and conditional acceptance, interruptions, manuscript examination, initial undated review letter, February 23, 1830 letter, November 2, 1831 acknowledgment, reader limit); Chapter XVI pp. 325–326 (later loss, outside-episode identity context in the source fold only).

Mary Somerville, A Preliminary Dissertation on the Mechanism of the Heavens (Philadelphia: Carey & Lea, 1832). https://www.gutenberg.org/files/67386/67386-h/67386-h.htm Title page and opening paragraphs defining physical astronomy and linking gravitation to planetary motions.

beats.text:
A visitor had come to speak with her at home. She was forty-six. He wanted her to explain a difficult book about the motion of the planets. Her husband joined him in asking her to try. She explained what the work required.

Its readers needed to know a kind of advanced mathematics. Before the main subject, she needed to prove problems about movement and the skies.

The original book had no diagrams. Readers already trained in its mathematics did not need them. For the book he wanted, she said, diagrams were necessary. She was describing the work to the two men asking for it.
beats.sourceNotes: One visit at her home, a few days after the March 27, 1827 request. Age is derived from the documented birth date. The conversation is a late-life recollection, probable in the fold. No exact room, posture, weather, or invented gesture is supplied.

beats.text:
In the conversation, she said she feared she could not do the task. The request had surprised her. She thought the visitor had mistaken how much she knew. Her knowledge had come through her own studies.

She believed it fell far short of the knowledge of men trained at universities. To write on this subject seemed too much to attempt. She doubted not only this book, but writing on any subject at all.

She had not had the university education she was comparing herself against.

She could describe the proofs the book needed. She could explain why its readers needed diagrams. That did not remove her stated fear about doing the work herself. The two men were asking her to try.

She was afraid she was incapable of the task.
beats.sourceNotes: The same conversation stays at the attested fear and assessment of her self-acquired knowledge. Inferiority is her belief, not the narrator's verdict. No new bodily symptom, shame, despair, humiliating remark, or rescue is invented. Later memory is probable.

beats.text:
She agreed to make the attempt. She promised to do her best. But she set conditions for the two men asking her. Her part in the work had to remain secret. If the manuscript failed, she wanted it destroyed.

The two conditions were part of her answer.

The agreement was to try the writing, with the possibility of failure still there. She had already explained the proofs and diagrams it needed. She did not claim she could make the whole subject simple for everyone.

She accepted the task with the condition of secrecy.
beats.sourceNotes: The small act is the remembered conditional agreement within the visit. No first page, instant new confidence, drafting location, written contract, or actual destruction is claimed. The limits she names remain present.

beats.text:
She rose early and arranged family work to leave time for writing. There were many interruptions. Her small room had no fireplace. In winter she had to write in the room where guests were received.

Visitors could arrive while she was in the middle of a difficult problem. They had come a long way to see her. She felt she had to receive them.

When the bell announced a visitor, she hid her papers to keep the work secret. She learned to leave a subject and resume it. She also taught her children, answering their questions beside her own work.

The writing took a considerable time. When it was finished, she sent the manuscript for examination and criticism. She was very nervous while it was being examined.
beats.sourceNotes: This compression uses attested recurring interruptions and a room without a fireplace, not an invented single visit. It ends with the completed manuscript under review. Mother's and daughter's late memories are probable; no unsupported duration, completed technical revision, or visitor motive is added.

beats.text:
The astronomer sent her a letter about the manuscript. He had read it with pleasure and admiration. He called it useful work. There were also points he wanted her to look at again.

One explanation of how forces act was unclear to him. He had marked it. His note concerned an explanation of a mathematical rule. On an early page, he had made another small note.

He thought this smaller point might hardly be worth a mark on the manuscript.

She was surprised that he had found so few errors. The letter made her happy and proud. The manuscript she had offered for examination had received his praise. It had also received his corrections.

The praise and the marked explanation were in the same reply. She preserved the letter.
beats.sourceNotes: The initial review letter supplies one letter-centered moment and its specific marked deficiency. Her remembered happiness, pride, surprise, and preservation are probable; the reproduced letter's contents are documented. No precise reading place/date, immediate storage gesture, or completed revision is invented.

beats.text:
Further criticism came in a later letter. The astronomer said the opening needed more space and fuller explanations. To him, her knowledge had led her to pass over difficulties for beginners.

He asked her to make the principles clearer. Some principles had been used before their basis was explained.

The book was published. A letter thanked her for copies sent to a college library and a learned society. Young students of mathematics could have access to it there.

The writer thought it could help them once they were able to read it. For general readers, only the opening part of the book was understandable. Reading the rest required a knowledge of advanced mathematics.

The difficult mathematics remained in the full book.
beats.sourceNotes: An open chronological move to the dated February 23, 1830 criticism and 1831 publication. The critic's assessment is not a diagnosis of her ability. No assertion that every recommendation was followed. The general-reader limit describes the book's content using her probable late assessment; the later separate printing after February 1832 is excluded. The narrative ends at 1831 publication/reception, with its access limit still present.

beats.text:
Her name was Mary Somerville.
She wrote a book explaining the mathematics behind the movements of the planets to people who wanted to understand the skies.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You do not have to feel certain about your work to care about it. You are allowed to have doubts.
beats.sourceNotes: Name, one plain role sentence, the fixed distance pair, and two declarative permission sentences. The used identity-context atom supplies separately located later family-loss context in the fold only, expressly outside the writing episode. Its combined confidence is conservatively probable; identity itself is supported by the title. No outcome promise, advice, comparative suffering, reader particulars, or diagnosis.
